summary: Defines SNMP management objects that expose the operation of a RADIUS authentication server, letting administrators monitor it. It was replaced by RFC 4669.

eli5.summary: A set of gauges on the machine that answers login questions, showing how many it answered and how many it turned away.

subtitle: Monitoring system objects for RADIUS authentication servers.

tldr.problem: Administrators running RADIUS authentication servers need to monitor the server's performance, see how many authentication requests it is handling, track errors, and diagnose problems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an SNMP MIB module that exposes the internal state and detailed statistics of a RADIUS authentication server, including counters for successful and failed authentications, duplicates, malformed requests, and bad authenticators.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can now use SNMP to remotely monitor RADIUS servers and track metrics like request volume, authentication acceptance rates, and error conditions. RFC 4669 replaced this standard.

facts.label: Client table
facts.value: 1 row per client, with 12 columns per row

today: RFC 2619 was a Proposed Standard for RADIUS server management. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4669, which updated the RADIUS server MIB.

sections.title: Monitoring RADIUS Servers
sections.content:
The RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) protocol is widely used by Internet Service Providers and network administrators to authenticate users who are trying to access the network. A RADIUS server sits at the center of this system, processing authentication requests from many different clients and making the final decision whether to grant or deny access.

Effectively managing a RADIUS server requires detailed visibility into its operation. Administrators need to know how many authentication requests the server is receiving, how many are being accepted or rejected, whether it is experiencing network problems, and whether requests are malformed or contain invalid authenticators. This RFC defines an SNMP MIB module that exposes all of these metrics and operational details.
sections.eli5: A RADIUS server is a machine that decides whether people are allowed to log into a network. The administrators running it need to see detailed statistics about what requests it receives, how many it approves or denies, and whether anything is going wrong.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The RADIUS Server MIB is a Management Information Base (MIB) module that conforms to SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information Version 2). It can be translated to SMIv1 for use with older SNMP implementations, though some features may be lost.

The MIB defines both server-wide scalar objects and a table of clients. The server-wide objects include the server's implementation identifier, how long the server has been running (uptime), when it was last reset, and a control object for resetting the server's configuration.

The MIB also tracks fourteen different server-level statistical counters, and for each RADIUS client that the server shares a secret with, it maintains a table with twelve columns of per-client statistics.
sections.eli5: SNMP is the way network managers peek inside machines to see what is happening. A MIB is a list of things you can look at. This one has general information about the server and detailed statistics for each client it talks to.

sections.title: Server Statistics and Client Counters
sections.content:
The server-level statistics track the overall workload and health of the RADIUS server. Key counters include the total number of Access-Request packets received on the authentication port, the number of invalid requests from unknown addresses, the number of duplicate requests, and the total counts of Access-Accept, Access-Reject, and Access-Challenge responses sent.

The MIB also tracks malformed requests, bad authenticators (integrity check failures), packets dropped for other reasons, and packets of unknown type. For each RADIUS client that the server shares a secret with, the RFC defines a table entry containing per-client statistics including the client's IP address, the port number the client uses, round-trip time estimates, and per-client counters of requests and responses.

These granular per-client statistics help administrators identify which clients are sending malformed requests, experiencing timeouts, or behaving unexpectedly.
sections.eli5: The server counts how many login requests it got, how many it accepted, rejected, or asked for more information. It also tracks when requests were broken, bad, or unknown. For each client machine that asks it questions, it keeps separate counters.

sections.title: Server Operation and Status Objects
sections.content:
The RFC defines a radiusAuthServConfigReset object that allows network administrators to command the server to reinitialize its persistent state as if it were just starting up. This provides a way to reset the server's configuration without a full restart. When read, the object returns the server's current state: other (unknown state), initializing (server reinitializing), or running (currently operational).

The MIB also tracks server uptime (how long the server process has been running) and reset time (how long since the server was last reset). These timing objects help administrators understand whether the server is stable or is restarting frequently.

These operational objects are read-write (unlike the client MIB statistics which are read-only), allowing administrators to trigger administrative actions remotely via SNMP.
sections.eli5: Administrators can use SNMP to tell the server to reload its settings without turning it off and back on. They can also see how long the server has been running and when it was last restarted, to know if it is stable.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
Like the RADIUS client MIB, the server MIB contains objects that should be protected from unauthorized access. The object that allows remote reset of the server should be carefully controlled, as an attacker who could trigger it could disrupt the server's operation.

Additionally, the identity, uptime, and statistical information about the server could be valuable to an attacker planning an attack. The RFC recommends implementing SNMPv3 with its User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model to ensure that only authorized administrators can query these objects and that the information is encrypted in transit. SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c provide no encryption or strong authentication, so they are not recommended for protecting this sensitive information.
sections.eli5: The server statistics contain information that attackers could use to plan an attack, and the reset function could be misused. You should use secure SNMP (SNMPv3) to keep this information private and only let authorized people use it.
